sources.title: What Causes the Seasons? (NASA Space Place)

publish.title: Why do we have seasons? It's not distance
publish.description: Seasons come from Earth's tilt, not from its distance to the Sun.

scenes.headline: Why do we have seasons?
scenes.narration: Is summer when Earth is closest to the Sun? Many people think so. It is not.

scenes.headline: It is not distance
scenes.narration: Earth is actually closest to the Sun in early January, in the middle of northern winter.

scenes.headline: The real reason
scenes.narration: The real reason is tilt. Earth's axis is tilted by about twenty-three point four degrees to its orbit.

scenes.headline: June and December
scenes.narration: In June the northern half tilts toward the Sun, with longer days and more direct light. In December it tilts away.

left.label: June, north
left.text: Tilted toward the Sun: long days

right.label: December, north
right.text: Tilted away: short days, slanted light

scenes.headline: Opposite seasons
scenes.narration: When it is summer in the north, it is winter in the south, because the two halves of Earth tilt toward and away from the Sun at opposite times.

scenes.headline: Look at the shadows
scenes.narration: Watch how your shadow changes through the year.
